summary: Adds two new fields to Sensor Measurement Lists (SenML) that indicate the content format of binary data values, that is, their Internet media type including parameters and any content codings. This helps processing of binary values in sensor data. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A sensor sends a mystery package, and now the package carries a label saying what kind of thing is inside.

subtitle: Two new SenML fields that say what kind of data is inside a binary sensor value.

tldr.problem: SenML records can carry arbitrary binary data in the Data Value field "vd", but a receiver far away in space or time may have no way to know how to interpret it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a "ct" field to a record and a "bct" base field that sets a default for many records. Each holds either a CoAP Content-Format number or a media type with optional parameters and content codings joined by "@".
tldr.outcome: Binary data in SenML can describe itself, so processors no longer depend on out-of-band knowledge. It is a Proposed Standard, not obsoleted.

today: RFC 9193 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2022 and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Binary Data Needs a Label
sections.content:
The Sensor Measurement Lists (SenML) media types (RFC 8428) carry numbers, text strings and arbitrary binary Data Values in the vd field. In the JSON form, binary data is base64url encoded without padding. The receiver is expected to know how to interpret it from context, such as the name of the data source, but that context may be lost when a Pack is passed along over time and through several entities.

This RFC lets a record state an Internet media type and, optionally, content codings right in the SenML Record. One way to name a format is the single unsigned integer of the CoAP Content-Format (RFC 7252), for example 60 for application/cbor.
sections.eli5: A sensor can send a sealed box with no label. This RFC adds a sticker that says what is in the box, so whoever opens it later knows what to do.

sections.title: Content Format Terminology
sections.content:
The RFC defines several closely related terms. A Content-Type is a media type name plus optional parameters. A content coding is a registered encoding transformation such as deflate or gzip, as in HTTP. A content format is a Content-Type plus zero or more content codings, identified either by a numeric Content-Format number from the CoAP registry or by a Content-Format-String.

A Content-Format-Spec is the string form of a content format: either a Content-Format-String or the decimal string of a Content-Format number. Readers should also know the concepts of RFC 8428. The RFC also notes that a SenML creator cannot know what every remote consumer understands, but a consumer will at least know when it needs to be updated to handle a value.
sections.eli5: A content format is the answer to 'what is this file and was it squashed or locked afterwards?'. It can be written as a short number or as a longer name.

sections.title: The Content-Format Field "ct"
sections.content:
When a record has a Data Value (vd), it MAY also include a Content-Format field with the label ct. Its value is a Content-Format-Spec, always carried as a string so its data type stays consistent. It is one of two things:

  • a CoAP Content-Format number in decimal with no leading zeros (except 0 itself), an unsigned integer in the range 0-65535;
  • a Content-Format-String with a Content-Type and zero or more content codings.

If the string contains only digits it is read as a Content-Format number. To add content codings, each coding value is appended to the Content-Type, separated by @, in the order they were applied, for example text/plain; charset=utf-8@deflate. With no @, no content coding applies and the identity coding is assumed.
sections.eli5: The label can be a short code number from a known list, or a written description. If the contents were squashed or locked, you add the steps after an at sign, in the order they were done.

sections.title: The Base Field "bct"
sections.content:
The Base Content-Format field, label bct, sets a default for ct. Its range covers the record that contains it, up to but not including the next record with a bct field, or to the end of the Pack. When the Pack is resolved (Section 4.6 of RFC 8428), the base value is added as ct to every record in range that has a vd field but no ct of its own.

That lets many records share one declaration while an individual record overrides it. In the RFC's example, the nfc-reader records resolve to base value 60, while the iris-photo record sets image/png itself.
sections.eli5: Instead of sticking the same label on every box, you put one label at the top of the pile. A box with its own label keeps its own.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
Section 6 gives ABNF for Content-Format-Spec strings. It has three new rules: Content-Format-Spec is a Content-Format-Number or a Content-Format-String; a Content-Format-Number is 0 or a nonzero digit followed by digits; and a Content-Format-String is a Content-Type followed by any number of @ and Content-Coding items.

The remaining rules are collected and adapted from other RFCs. The Content-Type rule is cleaned up from RFC 9110, keeping only the space character as blank space, and each parameter is a token, an equals sign, and a token or quoted string. A Content-Coding is a token.
sections.eli5: This is the exact grammar that says which label strings are allowed, so every program reads them the same way.

sections.title: Examples of Valid Values
sections.content:
The RFC lists valid values for ct and bct, including both numeric and string forms. The number form is compact, while the string form covers combinations that have no assigned number.

Notably, the value 0 stands for text/plain with charset utf-8, application/json is equivalent to 50, and application/json@deflate is equivalent to 11050. Several codings can be stacked, as in application/json@deflate@aes128gcm.
sections.eli5: Some labels are short code numbers, and some are longer words. The same thing can often be written either way, and stacking steps just means listing them in order.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Stating a media type does not exempt a consuming application from checking its input properly. An attacker who can supply crafted SenML data can pick the media types, which may expose vulnerabilities in the handlers for those types. The RFC specifically mentions "decompression bombs", compressed data crafted to expand to extremely large data items.
sections.eli5: A label on a box is only a claim. Always check what is really inside before you use it, and watch out for boxes that unfold into something enormous.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has assigned two new labels in the SenML Labels subregistry of the Sensor Measurement Lists registry: bct (Base Content-Format) and ct (Content-Format). Both have the JSON type String and the XML type string, with RFC 9193 as the reference.

Per RFC 8428, no CBOR labels and no Efficient XML Interchange (EXI) schemaId values are supplied.
sections.eli5: The official list of SenML field names got two new entries, one for the single-record label and one for the default label.
